title: Sinkholes: When the Ground Collapses
summary: How sinkholes form when rock underground slowly dissolves and the ground above suddenly or slowly sinks, and why some parts of Saudi Arabia must watch for them.
poll: The ground under your feet can feel solid even when it is secretly hollow underneath.

versions.title: When the Ground Sinks
versions.text:
One day, part of a road sinks. A hole opens. Wait! What made this happen?

This is a sinkhole. A sinkhole is a hole. The ground sinks down. It sinks into empty space. The name comes from "sink" and "hole."

How does a sinkhole form? Deep down, there is soft rock. Rain seeps in. It eats the rock. This makes a space.

The roof of this space gets thin. It can not hold up the ground. Then the ground can collapse. It drops into the hole.

Some sinkholes form slow. The ground just sinks slow. Some form fast. The ground falls all at once!

A sinkhole can be small. It can be huge. A big one can eat a tree. It can eat a road too.

In Saudi Arabia, some spots have soft rock. Sinkholes can form there too. People watch the ground to stay safe.

This hole is a sinkhole. A sinkhole is a hole in the ground. The ground sinks into empty space below. The name comes from "sink" and "hole."

How does a sinkhole form? Deep underground, there is often soft rock. Rain seeps down. It goes through cracks. It slowly eats away at the rock. This leaves an empty space below.

Over time, the roof of this space grows thin. It gets weak. It can not hold up the ground. Then the ground can collapse. It falls down into the space.

Some sinkholes form slow. The ground just sinks slow. Others form fast. The ground collapses at once.

A sinkhole can be small, or it can be huge. A large one can swallow a tree or a road.

In Saudi Arabia, some spots have this kind of soft rock. Sinkholes can form there too. People watch the ground to stay safe.

This hole is called a sinkhole. A sinkhole is a hole or a dip in the ground. It forms when the surface sinks down into empty space below it. The word sinkhole comes from two simple words, "sink" and "hole," since the ground truly does sink.

In Saudi Arabia, some areas have this kind of soft, limestone rock. Sinkholes can, and sometimes do, form there too. Scientists study and map the ground in these areas to help keep people safe.

versions.title: Sinkholes: When the Ground Collapses
versions.text:
Imagine a quiet morning in a small town. Suddenly, part of a field sinks down. A deep hole opens in the ground. What could cause something so strange?

This hole is called a sinkhole. A sinkhole is a hole in the ground. It forms when the surface sinks into an empty space below it. The word combines "sink" and "hole," since that is just what the ground does.

Sinkholes usually form because of soft rock underground, such as limestone. Rainwater seeps down through tiny cracks. This water is a little acidic. Over a long time, it slowly dissolves the soft rock. This leaves a hollow cavity underground.

As the years pass, the roof of this space grows thin and weak. It can not hold up the heavy ground above. The ground then collapses. It falls suddenly down into the empty space below.

There are two main kinds of sinkholes. One kind forms slowly, as the surface just slowly sinks over many years. The other kind forms fast, when the roof of the space suddenly gives way, sometimes with no warning.

A sinkhole can be tiny, or it can be huge. A large sinkhole can swallow a tree, a road, or even a whole building. Places with lots of limestone underground are extra likely to have sinkholes.

Certain areas of Saudi Arabia sit on this soft, limestone ground. Sinkholes can and do form there too. Pumping too much groundwater can also make a collapse more likely. Geologists study the ground to warn people and keep them safe.

versions.title: Sinkholes: When the Ground Collapses
versions.text:
Imagine a quiet morning in a small town, when a peculiar thing happens: part of a field sinks downward and a deep hole suddenly opens in the ground, seemingly without any cause. What could possibly explain something so unusual, and why does it so often seem to happen without any warning at all?

This hole is known as a sinkhole, a depression in the ground that forms whenever the surface sinks into an empty space that lies below it. The word sinkhole simply combines "sink" and "hole," since that is precisely what the ground does above a hidden, hollow cavity that has been quietly growing out of sight.

Sinkholes usually form because of soft underground rock, such as limestone, a type of rock that dissolves fairly easily in water over time. Rainwater seeps downward through tiny cracks in the ground, and because this water is slightly acidic, it gradually dissolves the soft rock below through a slow process called erosion, leaving behind a hollow cavity underground that continues to widen year after year.

As the years pass, the roof of this cavity grows progressively thinner and weaker, resting on an increasingly unstable foundation of partly dissolved rock. Eventually it becomes too weak to support the considerable weight of the ground above it, and the ground then collapses, falling suddenly down into the empty space below, sometimes carrying whatever sat on the surface along with it.

Geologists describe two main kinds of sinkholes. A solution sinkhole forms through a gradual process, as the surface slowly sinks downward over many years without much visible warning. A collapse sinkhole forms rapidly instead, when the roof of a cavity suddenly gives way all at once, often catching nearby residents completely by surprise.

A sinkhole can be tiny, or it can be absolutely enormous, capable of swallowing a tree, a road, or even an entire building within a matter of seconds. Regions with abundant limestone underground are called karst landscapes, and because so much of their rock is prone to dissolving, these regions are especially susceptible to sinkholes forming again and again across the centuries.

Certain areas of Saudi Arabia rest on karst, limestone ground, so sinkholes can and do occasionally form there, particularly after unusually heavy rainfall has soaked deep into the rock below. Pumping excessive groundwater can also lower the water table that once helped support a cavity's roof and foundation, removing a kind of hidden cushion and making a sudden collapse considerably more likely. Geologists carefully study and map such ground using surveys and underground sensors, in order to warn people and help keep them safe long before any visible sign of trouble ever appears on the surface above.

MID.prompt: Explain why pumping too much groundwater can make a sinkhole more likely in some places. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I gave a clear answer to the question.
I used at least two details from the article.
I explained how the details connect to each other.
MID.modelAnswer: Pumping too much groundwater can make a sinkhole more likely because it removes water that was quietly helping to support the ground above an underground cavity. One detail is that sinkholes often form above a hollow cavity created when rainwater slowly dissolves soft rock, such as limestone. Another detail is that the roof of this cavity can already be thin and weak after many years of dissolving rock. When groundwater that was helping hold up this weak roof is pumped away too quickly, the roof can lose even more support and collapse sooner than it otherwise would have.

HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that sinkholes always happen suddenly with no way to predict them. The article explains that most sinkholes form through a gradual process of erosion, in which slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves soft rock, such as limestone, over a very long period of time, which means geologists can often identify at-risk areas in advance. In addition, the article states that geologists carefully study and map ground in regions with karst, limestone terrain in order to warn people before a collapse happens. While a collapse sinkhole can give way suddenly once its roof becomes too weak, the underlying process that creates the danger develops gradually and can often be studied and tracked beforehand.
